assumption_register.statement: Per-requirement evaluators are deterministic given K and EC.

sources.note: Step 93: models failure/recovery within the same mathematical framework (recovery is itself a governed transition). Covers transaction-boundary vs real-world side effects, outbox pattern, durability, write-ahead logging/event sourcing with event validation before append, checkpointing, idempotent retry and exactly-once-as-semantic-effect, partial failure with never-infer-from-absence (three-valued), compensation vs rollback with compensation provenance, recovery-must-not-erase-history, failure as observation vs cause as inference, recovery confidence/freshness, reconciliation, monotonic recovery (no silent downgrade), RPO/RTO and multi-dimensional recovery assurance, failure-domain independence, and fault-injection/chaos testing. Closely related to concurrency-idempotency-replay-model.

rows.anchor: Step 92 established concurrent/distributed correctness. But real systems fail ... Can KnowledgeOS recover from failure without creating a state that violates its mathematical model? Failure ⇏ Semantic Corruption.
rows.statement: Frames Step 93's central requirement: Failure ⇏ Semantic Corruption — KnowledgeOS must recover from failure without violating its mathematical model.

lineage_claims.quote: Step 92 established that KnowledgeOS must remain semantically correct under concurrent and distributed execution.

rows.anchor: 93.1 — Failure is part of the state space ... S_0 -a-> S_partial -failure-> S_f. The system must define whether S_f is valid.
rows.statement: Extends the state model to include failure explicitly: S_0 --a--> S_partial --failure--> S_f, requiring the system to define whether S_f is valid.

rows.anchor: 93.2 — Experiment 1: interrupted transition ... Submitted→Approved. Crash occurs after step 1 (create approval). State: ApprovalExists=True but Status=Submitted. Expected: the intermediate state must either be valid by design or recoverable. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 1: a crash after only the first of three approval steps leaves ApprovalExists=True/Status=Submitted, which must be either valid-by-design or recoverable; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.3 — Atomic transaction ... T=(createApproval,updateStatus,emitRequiredState). Failure can cause T→Rollback. The system returns to S_0.
rows.statement: Defines wrapping the multi-step approval as one atomic transaction T so failure causes rollback to S_0.

rows.anchor: 93.4 — Experiment 2 ... Transaction fails before commit. Expected: S_after=S_before. Result: PASS. This is the classical atomicity property.
rows.statement: Experiment 2 confirms the classical atomicity property: a pre-commit failure leaves S_after=S_before; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.5 — But not everything is transactional ... commits database state, sends an external email, crashes. The database can roll back only its own state. The external email cannot necessarily be recalled.
rows.statement: Warns that non-transactional side effects (e.g. a sent email) cannot be rolled back along with the database, even though the database transaction can.

rows.anchor: 93.6 — Experiment 3 ... Database says Approved=True. Email was sent 'request rejected.' Expected: system has inconsistent external observations. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 3: a database recording Approved=True while an already-sent email said 'rejected' creates inconsistent external observations; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.7 — Transaction boundary ... TransactionBoundary ≠ EntireRealWorld. A database transaction protects only the resources participating in it.
rows.statement: States TransactionBoundary ≠ EntireRealWorld: a database transaction protects only its own participating resources, not external side effects.

rows.anchor: 93.8 — Outbox pattern ... commit BusinessState+EventToPublish in the same local transaction. Then Outbox→MessageBroker. The external event is published after durable state exists.
rows.statement: Describes the outbox pattern: committing BusinessState+EventToPublish atomically, then publishing from the outbox to a message broker after durable state exists.

rows.anchor: 93.9 — Experiment 4 ... Transaction commits Approved=True and ApprovalEvent exists in an outbox. Process crashes before publication. Expected: recovery can publish the event later. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 4: a crash before outbox event publication permits later recovery-driven publication; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.10 — Durability ... Does committed state survive failure? If Commit(S_1) occurs, after restart we expect Recover()→S_1.
rows.statement: Defines durability: committed state S_1 must be recoverable (Recover()→S_1) after a failure/restart.

rows.anchor: 93.11 — Experiment 5 ... System confirms Commit=True. Power failure occurs immediately afterward. After restart: Status=Submitted. Expected: DurabilityViolation. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 5: a confirmed commit reverting to Status=Submitted after a power failure is DurabilityViolation; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.12 — Recovery function ... R(F,S) as the recovery process following failure F. We want R(F,S) ∈ ValidStates.
rows.statement: Defines the recovery function R(F,S), requiring R(F,S) ∈ ValidStates.

rows.anchor: 93.13 — Experiment 6 ... System crashes in an intermediate state. Recovery reconstructs a state satisfying I(S)=True. Expected: RecoveryCorrect. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 6: recovery reconstructing a state satisfying I(S)=True from an intermediate crash is RecoveryCorrect; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.14 — Recovery is a mathematical transition ... Recovery is not merely infrastructure. It is itself a transition S_failed-recover->S_recovered. Recovery must obey the same semantic invariants.
rows.statement: States recovery is itself a mathematical transition S_failed --recover--> S_recovered, subject to the same semantic invariants as any other transition.

rows.anchor: 93.15 — Experiment 7 ... Normal business transitions preserve I. Recovery process reconstructs state without checking I. Expected: potential invariant violation. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 7: a recovery process that reconstructs state without checking invariant I risks invariant violation; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.16 — Crash consistency ... state A,B,C. A transaction updates all three. A crash may occur between writes if atomicity is absent. If A'=A1,B'=B1,C'=C0 is impossible under the model, I(A',B',C')=False.
rows.statement: Defines crash consistency: partial multi-field updates (A'=A1,B'=B1,C'=C0) that the model considers impossible violate I(A',B',C')=False.

rows.anchor: 93.17 — Experiment 8 ... Crash creates Approved=True but ApprovalRecord=False. Expected: recovery must repair or reject the state. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 8: a crash-created state with Approved=True but ApprovalRecord=False must be repaired or rejected by recovery; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.18 — Write-ahead logging ... Log(T)→Apply(T)→Commit. After crash: Recover(Log).
rows.statement: Describes write-ahead logging: Log(T)→Apply(T)→Commit, with crash recovery via Recover(Log).

rows.anchor: 93.19 — Experiment 9 ... Committed operation appears in durable log but not yet in materialized state. Expected: recovery can replay the operation. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 9: a logged-but-not-materialized committed operation can be replayed on recovery; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.20 — Event sourcing ... E_1,...,E_n. S_n=Fold(E_1,...,E_n). Recovery can reconstruct state from events.
rows.statement: Restates event sourcing (S_n=Fold(E_1..E_n)) as a mechanism for reconstructing state from an authoritative event sequence.

rows.anchor: 93.21 — Experiment 10 ... Materialized state is corrupted. Event history remains intact. Expected: S_reconstructed=Fold(E_1,...,E_n). Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 10: an intact event history can reconstruct a corrupted materialized state via Fold; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.22 — But event sourcing does not automatically solve semantics ... If an invalid event was written E_bad, replaying it reproduces the invalid state.
rows.statement: Warns event sourcing does not guarantee semantic correctness: replaying a previously-written invalid event (E_bad) reproduces the invalid state.

rows.anchor: 93.23 — Experiment 11 ... Event log contains UnauthorizedApproval. Replay faithfully reconstructs it. Expected: event durability does not imply event correctness. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 11: faithfully replaying a durably-logged UnauthorizedApproval event shows event durability does not imply event correctness; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.24 — Therefore event validation is required ... Validate(E,S). Valid(E,S) ⇒ Append(E).
rows.statement: States events must be validated (Validate(E,S)) before being appended: Valid(E,S) ⇒ Append(E).

rows.anchor: 93.25 — Checkpointing ... replaying 10^9 events may be expensive. Periodically create Checkpoint(S_k). Then recover from Checkpoint_k + E_{k+1}..E_n.
rows.statement: Defines checkpointing: periodic Checkpoint(S_k) plus subsequent events (E_{k+1}..E_n) enables faster recovery than replaying the full event history.

rows.anchor: 93.26 — Experiment 12 ... One million events exist. Checkpoint at event 999,000. Recovery requires only 1,000 events. Expected: recovery becomes significantly faster. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 12: checkpointing at event 999,000 of 1,000,000 makes recovery replay only 1,000 events, significantly faster; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.27 — Checkpoint integrity ... the checkpoint itself becomes an authoritative derived artifact. Checkpoint must have version, timestamp, source event position, integrity information, model version where relevant.
rows.statement: States a checkpoint is itself an authoritative derived artifact requiring version, timestamp, source event position, integrity information, and model version metadata.

rows.anchor: 93.28 — Experiment 13 ... Checkpoint says EventOffset=999000. But actual replay begins from 998500. Expected: duplicate or inconsistent reconstruction risk. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 13: a checkpoint's stated offset (999000) mismatching the actual replay start (998500) risks duplicate or inconsistent reconstruction; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.29 — Retry semantics ... Execute(A) times out. The caller does not know whether A actually executed. It retries.
rows.statement: Illustrates retry ambiguity: a timed-out Execute(A) leaves the caller uncertain whether A executed, prompting a retry.

rows.anchor: 93.30 — Experiment 14 ... First request succeeds remotely but response is lost. Second request arrives. Expected: without idempotency or deduplication, the operation may execute twice. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 14: a lost-response retry without idempotency/deduplication can execute the operation twice; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.31 — Idempotency becomes a recovery invariant ... f(f(S))=f(S). This is extremely valuable under retry.
rows.statement: States idempotency (f(f(S))=f(S)) becomes an especially valuable recovery invariant under retry.

rows.anchor: 93.32 — Experiment 15 ... Approve(request) is retried three times. Expected: one semantic approval. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 15: retrying Approve(request) three times should produce exactly one semantic approval; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.33 — Exactly-once is often semantic ... ExactlyOnceSemanticEffect achieved through CommandID and Deduplication, rather than requiring perfect transport-level exactly-once delivery.
rows.statement: States exactly-once semantics is usually achieved via CommandID+Deduplication for a semantic effect, not perfect transport-level exactly-once delivery.

rows.anchor: 93.34 — Experiment 16 ... Three copies of CommandID=42 arrive. Expected: one semantic effect. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 16: three duplicate CommandID=42 deliveries should produce one semantic effect via deduplication; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.35 — Partial failure ... A→B→C→D. A and B succeed. C fails. D never executes. The system is now in a partial state.
rows.statement: Defines partial failure in a workflow A→B→C→D where an intermediate step (C) fails, leaving a partial state.

rows.anchor: 93.36 — Experiment 17 ... Workflow state A=True, B=True, C=False, D=Unknown. Expected: workflow must explicitly represent partial completion. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 17: a partial workflow state (A=True,B=True,C=False,D=Unknown) must be explicitly represented; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.37 — Never infer completion from absence ... If D did not execute, that does not mean D=False unless the system knows that execution was attempted and failed. It may be Unknown.
rows.statement: States the never-infer-completion-from-absence principle: D not having executed does not mean D=False unless attempted-and-failed is known; otherwise D=Unknown.

rows.anchor: 93.38 — Experiment 18 ... Network fails before receiving the response from D. Expected: D=Unknown rather than D=False. Result: PASS. This again connects to our three-valued epistemic model.
rows.statement: Experiment 18: a network failure before D's response arrives means D=Unknown, not D=False, reinforcing the three-valued epistemic model; result PASS.

lineage_claims.quote: This again connects to our three-valued epistemic model.

rows.anchor: 93.39 — Compensation ... A cannot be rolled back technically. We may execute A^-1 as a compensating operation. But A^-1 may not restore the exact original state.
rows.statement: Defines compensation A^-1 for a technically-irreversible action A, noting it may not restore the exact original state.

rows.anchor: 93.40 — Experiment 19 ... Original S_0. After action S_1. Compensation produces S_2 where S_2≠S_0. Expected: compensation is not equivalent to rollback. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 19: a compensation producing S_2≠S_0 confirms compensation is not equivalent to rollback; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.41 — Compensation provenance ... OriginalAction, FailureReason, CompensationAction, ResidualDifference.
rows.statement: Defines required compensation-provenance fields: OriginalAction, FailureReason, CompensationAction, ResidualDifference.

rows.anchor: 93.42 — Experiment 20 ... A deployment was partially executed and later compensated. Expected: history preserves both DeploymentAttempt and Compensation. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 20: a partially-executed-then-compensated deployment must preserve both DeploymentAttempt and Compensation in history; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.43 — Recovery must not erase history ... if history is erased, we lose evidence that the failure occurred.
rows.statement: Warns recovery repairing an invalid state must not erase historical evidence that the failure occurred.

rows.anchor: 93.44 — Experiment 21 ... System reaches InvalidState. Recovery restores ValidState. Audit log shows only the final state. Expected: insufficient forensic provenance. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 21: an audit log showing only the final (recovered) state, not the prior invalid state, is insufficient forensic provenance; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.45 — Distinguish state from history ... CurrentState and StateHistory. Recovery can restore current state while preserving historical evidence.
rows.statement: Distinguishes CurrentState from StateHistory, so recovery can restore current state while preserving historical evidence of failure.

rows.anchor: 93.46 — Failure itself is an observation ... FailureEvent as part of the knowledge model. F=(component,time,operation,state,cause?,impact). Cause may remain Unknown.
rows.statement: Defines FailureEvent F=(component,time,operation,state,cause?,impact) as part of the knowledge model, with cause potentially Unknown.

rows.anchor: 93.47 — Experiment 22 ... Service crashes. Root cause is not yet established. Expected: FailureObserved=True but Cause=Unknown. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 22: a crashed service with unestablished root cause is FailureObserved=True, Cause=Unknown; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.48 — Root cause is an inference ... P(Cause=X)=0.8. That does not change the original failure fact. It adds an inference.
rows.statement: States a later probabilistic root-cause estimate (P(Cause=X)=0.8) is an added inference, not a change to the original failure fact.

rows.anchor: 93.49 — Experiment 23 ... 'Service crashed at 14:03.' 'Memory pressure probably caused the crash.' Expected: both remain distinct: Observation ≠ Hypothesis. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 23: an original crash observation and a later causal hypothesis must remain distinct: Observation ≠ Hypothesis; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.50 — Recovery confidence ... RecoveryVerified versus RecoveryBestEffort.
rows.statement: Distinguishes RecoveryVerified from RecoveryBestEffort as different recovery assurance levels.

rows.anchor: 93.51 — Experiment 24 ... System restores a database from backup. Integrity check passes. Expected: higher confidence. If no integrity check occurs, RecoveryConfidence must remain lower. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 24: a backup restoration with a passing integrity check warrants higher recovery confidence than one without; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.52 — Backup is not automatically valid knowledge ... stale, incomplete, corrupted, inconsistent, taken before a critical event. Backup ≠ Truth.
rows.statement: States Backup ≠ Truth: a backup may be stale, incomplete, corrupted, inconsistent, or predate a critical event.

rows.anchor: 93.53 — Experiment 25 ... Backup timestamp t_0. Critical decision occurred t_1>t_0. Recovery restores from t_0. Expected: KnowledgeOS must recognize missing knowledge between t_0 and t_1. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 25: restoring from a backup taken at t_0 before a critical decision at t_1 leaves a recognized knowledge gap between t_0 and t_1; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.54 — Recovery creates an epistemic boundary ... After restoring from backup, the system knows K(t_0). It does not automatically know K(t_1). RecoveredState ≠ AutomaticallyCurrentState.
rows.statement: States RecoveredState ≠ AutomaticallyCurrentState: restoring K(t_0) does not automatically confer knowledge of K(t_1).

rows.anchor: 93.55 — Experiment 26 ... Backup restored successfully. System immediately labels itself Current=True. Expected: potentially incorrect until post-recovery synchronization/reconciliation occurs. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 26: a system labeling itself Current=True immediately after backup restoration, before reconciliation, is potentially incorrect; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.56 — Reconciliation ... RecoveredState may need to be compared with surviving systems S_A,S_B,S_C. Then Reconciliation identifies discrepancies.
rows.statement: Defines reconciliation: comparing RecoveredState with surviving systems to identify discrepancies.

rows.anchor: 93.57 — Experiment 27 ... Recovered database says Version=100. External service says Version=105. Expected: ReconciliationRequired. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 27: a version mismatch (100 vs 105) between recovered and external systems triggers ReconciliationRequired; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.58 — Recovery should be monotonic where possible ... recovery should ideally avoid silently replacing valid knowledge K_t with weaker or less certain knowledge. K_recovered should preserve the strongest trustworthy evidence available.
rows.statement: States recovery should be monotonic where possible: it should not silently replace stronger knowledge with weaker/older knowledge, preserving the strongest trustworthy evidence available.

rows.anchor: 93.59 — Experiment 28 ... System has durable evidence from another source showing PolicyVersion=105. Backup restores PolicyVersion=100. Expected: the system should not blindly downgrade authoritative knowledge to version 100. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 28: a backup restoring an older PolicyVersion=100 must not silently override durable evidence of PolicyVersion=105 from elsewhere; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.60 — Disaster recovery ... Primary and Secondary. Failover becomes Primary→Secondary.
rows.statement: Defines disaster recovery failover Primary→Secondary at larger infrastructure scale.

rows.anchor: 93.61 — Experiment 29 ... Primary fails. Secondary has stale state. Expected: failover must account for ReplicationLag. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 29: a stale secondary during failover must account for ReplicationLag; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.62 — Recovery point objective ... RPO as the maximum acceptable loss of recent state. If RPO=5min, then losing 30min of knowledge violates the requirement.
rows.statement: Defines Recovery Point Objective (RPO): the maximum acceptable state loss; e.g. RPO=5min violated by a 30min loss.

rows.anchor: 93.63 — Experiment 30 ... Required RPO=5min. Actual RPO=30min. Expected: RecoveryRequirementViolation. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 30: an actual RPO of 30min against a required 5min is RecoveryRequirementViolation; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.64 — Recovery time objective ... RTO as the maximum acceptable recovery time. If RTO=15min and recovery takes 2h, the system violates its operational contract.
rows.statement: Defines Recovery Time Objective (RTO): the maximum acceptable recovery duration; e.g. RTO=15min violated by a 2h recovery.

rows.anchor: 93.65 — Experiment 31 ... Expected: RecoveryTime≤RTO. Actual: RecoveryTime>RTO. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 31 confirms an actual RecoveryTime exceeding RTO is a violation; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.66 — Recovery assurance is multi-dimensional ... Correctness+Completeness+Freshness+Provenance+Availability. Not simply 'the server came back.'
rows.statement: States recovery assurance is multi-dimensional (Correctness+Completeness+Freshness+Provenance+Availability), not simply whether the server came back.

rows.anchor: 93.67 — Failure-domain awareness ... A resilient KnowledgeOS should avoid placing all critical knowledge in the same failure domain. If Evidence and Backup exist on the same failed infrastructure, the backup is not independent.
rows.statement: Warns against co-locating Evidence and Backup in the same failure domain, since a shared failure domain makes the backup non-independent.

rows.anchor: 93.68 — Experiment 32 ... Primary and backup storage fail simultaneously. Expected: the architecture has not achieved true independent recovery. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 32: simultaneous primary and backup storage failure shows the architecture lacks true independent recovery; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.69 — Independent evidence sources ... redundancy across Storage_1, Storage_2, Repository, AuditLog. But correlated copies are not independent evidence.
rows.statement: States that redundancy across multiple storage systems is only meaningful if the copies are genuinely independent, not merely correlated replicas.

rows.anchor: 93.70 — Experiment 33 ... Three replicas are all created from one corrupted source. Expected: three replicas do not provide three independent confirmations. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 33: three replicas of one corrupted source do not provide three independent confirmations; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.71 — Fault injection ... reliability cannot be established merely by saying 'we have retries.' We need experiments: FailureInjection→Recovery→InvariantCheck.
rows.statement: States reliability requires empirical FailureInjection→Recovery→InvariantCheck experiments, not just an assertion of having retries.

rows.anchor: 93.72 — Experiment 34 ... Inject failure at every stage of A→B→C. For each failure point I(S_recovered)=True. Expected: recovery test passes only if the invariant survives every tested interruption. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 34: recovery tests must pass I(S_recovered)=True for every failure-injection point across A→B→C; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.73 — Chaos testing ... network partitions, process crashes, delayed/duplicate messages, database/storage failures, service unavailability. Empirical validation of failure invariants.
rows.statement: Describes chaos testing (network partitions, process crashes, delayed/duplicate messages, database/storage failures, service unavailability) as empirical validation of failure invariants, not chaos for its own sake.

rows.anchor: 93.74 — Experiment 35 ... Normal tests pass. Failure-injection test reveals UnauthorizedState after recovery. Expected: architecture requires correction. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 35: a failure-injection test revealing UnauthorizedState after recovery (despite passing normal tests) requires architecture correction; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.75 — The strongest recovery invariant ... I_Recovery: for every supported failure mode F, recovery must either restore a valid state, or explicitly enter a declared degraded/unknown state. The system must never silently fabricate validity.
rows.statement: States the strongest recovery invariant I_Recovery: for every supported failure mode, recovery must restore a valid state or explicitly enter a declared degraded/unknown state — never silently fabricate validity.

rows.anchor: 93.76 — Degraded state ... State=Degraded. EvidenceFreshness=Unknown. This is preferable to EvidenceFreshness=Current.
rows.statement: Defines a Degraded state (e.g. EvidenceFreshness=Unknown), preferable to falsely claiming EvidenceFreshness=Current.

rows.anchor: 93.77 — Experiment 36 ... Recovery cannot verify whether the restored policy is current. Expected: PolicyFreshness=Unknown. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 36: recovery unable to verify policy currency should report PolicyFreshness=Unknown; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 93.78 — New invariants: I_AtomicRecovery, I_Durability, I_RecoveryValidity, I_FailureHistory, I_Reconciliation, I_RecoveryFreshness, I_RetrySafety, I_Compensation, I_FailureEpistemics, I_RecoveryAssurance
rows.statement: States nine further new invariants: I_AtomicRecovery (failed atomic transitions must not leave semantically invalid committed states), I_Durability (a committed authoritative state must remain recoverable per its durability contract), I_RecoveryValidity (recovery must produce a valid state or explicitly degraded/unknown state), I_FailureHistory (recovery must not silently erase evidence of failure/partial execution/compensation), I_Reconciliation (recovered state must be reconciled with surviving authoritative state where divergence is possible), I_RecoveryFreshness (a recovered state must not be represented as current unless freshness is established), I_RetrySafety (retryable operations must have explicit duplicate-execution semantics), I_Compensation (compensation must remain distinguishable from perfect rollback and preserve residual effects), I_FailureEpistemics (observed failure, inferred cause, and unresolved cause must remain distinct knowledge states), I_RecoveryAssurance (recovery assurance must include correctness, completeness, freshness, and provenance appropriate to criticality).

rows.anchor: 93.79 — Step 93 verdict: STEP 93 — PASS ... Normal→Failure→Recovery→Reconciliation. Failure is not outside the mathematical model. Failure is itself a possible transition in the system.
rows.statement: Records Step 93 verdict PASS: the model explicitly encompasses Normal→Failure→Recovery→Reconciliation; failure is itself a possible transition within the mathematical model, not outside it.

rows.anchor: The KnowledgeOS state machine is becoming much more complete ... S=(Knowledge,Evidence,Policy,Authority,Decision,Execution,Version,Time,Causality,Health). Transitions include Learn, Infer, Decide, Authorize, Execute, but also Fail, Retry, Rollback, Compensate, Recover, Reconcile.
rows.statement: Extends the KnowledgeOS state tuple to S=(Knowledge,Evidence,Policy,Authority,Decision,Execution,Version,Time,Causality,Health) with transitions including Fail/Retry/Rollback/Compensate/Recover/Reconcile alongside Learn/Infer/Decide/Authorize/Execute.

rows.anchor: The deeper result ... A KnowledgeOS invariant must survive not only normal execution, but also concurrency and supported failure/recovery paths. 'The architecture preserves its declared semantics across normal, concurrent, and failure states within its declared assumptions.'
rows.statement: States the deeper architecture-correctness requirement: invariants must survive normal execution, concurrency, and supported failure/recovery paths within declared assumptions — testable and verifiable, unlike 'the architecture works when everything works'.

rows.anchor: Step 94 — Next boundary: security, adversarial behavior and trust ... some actors may be Adversarial: forge evidence, manipulate provenance, bypass authorization, poison knowledge, exploit race conditions, create contradictory states, manipulate AI agents, inject false instructions, corrupt retrieva
rows.statement: Previews Step 94: moving from faulty/unavailable actors to actively Adversarial ones (forging evidence, manipulating provenance, bypassing authorization, poisoning knowledge, exploiting race conditions, manipulating AI agents, etc.), asking whether invariants survive active attack; covers Security, Trust, Adversarial Models, Integrity, Authentication, Authorization, Knowledge Poisoning, AI Agent Security, Trust Boundaries.

lexical.anchor: Step 92 established concurrent/distributed correctness. But real systems fail ... Can KnowledgeOS recover from failure without creating a state that violates its mathematical model? Failure ⇏ Semantic Corruption.

conceptual.anchor: 93.73 — Chaos testing ... network partitions, process crashes, delayed/duplicate messages, database/storage failures, service unavailability. Empirical validation of failure invariants.

formal.anchor: 93.1 — Failure is part of the state space ... S_0 -a-> S_partial -failure-> S_f. The system must define whether S_f is valid.

operational.anchor: 93.2 — Experiment 1: interrupted transition ... Submitted→Approved. Crash occurs after step 1 (create approval). State: ApprovalExists=True but Status=Submitted. Expected: the intermediate state must either be valid by design or recoverable. Result: PASS

rationale_evidence.anchor: Step 92 established concurrent/distributed correctness. But real systems fail ... Can KnowledgeOS recover from failure without creating a state that violates its mathematical model? Failure ⇏ Semantic Corruption.
rationale_evidence.statement: Frames Step 93's central requirement: Failure ⇏ Semantic Corruption — KnowledgeOS must recover from failure without violating its mathematical model.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 93.5 — But not everything is transactional ... commits database state, sends an external email, crashes. The database can roll back only its own state. The external email cannot necessarily be recalled.
rationale_evidence.statement: Warns that non-transactional side effects (e.g. a sent email) cannot be rolled back along with the database, even though the database transaction can.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 93.16 — Crash consistency ... state A,B,C. A transaction updates all three. A crash may occur between writes if atomicity is absent. If A'=A1,B'=B1,C'=C0 is impossible under the model, I(A',B',C')=False.
rationale_evidence.statement: Defines crash consistency: partial multi-field updates (A'=A1,B'=B1,C'=C0) that the model considers impossible violate I(A',B',C')=False.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 93.29 — Retry semantics ... Execute(A) times out. The caller does not know whether A actually executed. It retries.
rationale_evidence.statement: Illustrates retry ambiguity: a timed-out Execute(A) leaves the caller uncertain whether A executed, prompting a retry.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 93.69 — Independent evidence sources ... redundancy across Storage_1, Storage_2, Repository, AuditLog. But correlated copies are not independent evidence.
rationale_evidence.statement: States that redundancy across multiple storage systems is only meaningful if the copies are genuinely independent, not merely correlated replicas.

aliases: Bounded-Context Translation, Semantic Mapping, Conceptual Alignment and Knowledge Interoperability

sources.note: S0932's Step 39: formalizes cross-bounded-context knowledge translation as non-invertible, typed, contract-bearing, purpose/use-case-relative operations distinct from identity/merging, with explicit loss tracking, versioning, drift, and the semantic-vs-factual-conflict distinction. This file's own opening presupposes Step 38 content not yet processed in this batch's file order, confirming a further step-number deviation (Step 39 placed before Step 38).

rows.anchor: Customer_Sales and Customer_Billing refer to the same real-world organization. It does not follow that Customer_Sales=Customer_Billing ... How can knowledge cross a bounded-context boundary without corrupting meaning?
rows.statement: Poses the bounded-context-translation problem, distinguishing it from entity-identity questions.

lineage_claims.quote: We continue from Step 38. Step 38 established: Similarity != Identity and Reference != Entity.

rows.anchor: x_C. Its meaning is Meaning(x|C). Meaning(x|C_1) != Meaning(x|C_2) is perfectly legitimate
rows.statement: Formalizes context-relative concept meaning.

rows.anchor: Ref(x_C1)=r and Ref(x_C2)=r. SameRealWorldReferent does not imply SameDomainConcept. This is one of the most important principles in the entire architecture
rows.statement: States one of the architecture's most important principles: shared real-world referent does not imply shared domain concept.

rows.anchor: Customer_Sales: customerNumber, salesStatus, salesRegion, accountManager. Customer_Billing: debtorNumber, creditLimit, paymentStatus, invoiceAddress. The two models overlap. But they do not have the same semantics
rows.statement: Worked Customer_Sales vs Customer_Billing example of overlapping but non-identical bounded-context models.

rows.anchor: T_{A->B}: K_A -> K_B where K_A and K_B are knowledge structures within bounded contexts
rows.statement: Formally defines the translation function between bounded-context knowledge structures.

rows.anchor: Customer_Sales -> Customer_Billing may discard salesRegion. T_{B->A}(T_{A->B}(x)) != x. Translation != bijection
rows.statement: Worked counterexample showing translation is generally non-invertible/non-bijective.

rows.anchor: TranslationType in {Lossless, Lossy, Approximate, Partial, Invalid}. This classification should be explicit
rows.statement: Defines a five-way translation-type taxonomy that must be made explicit.

rows.anchor: If T(x) preserves all relevant semantics under the target context: Meaning(T(x)|B)=Meaning(x|A) for the relevant semantic dimensions. Then translation is effectively lossless for that purpose
rows.statement: Defines purpose-relative lossless translation.

rows.anchor: A={a1,a2,a3,a4} but target context only supports {b1,b2}. Then T(A) must discard information. That is acceptable if explicitly represented
rows.statement: Worked example of acceptable lossy translation conditional on explicit representation of the loss.

rows.anchor: If T drops information, KnowledgeOS should preserve Loss(T). Otherwise a downstream consumer may incorrectly believe the translated object contains the complete original semantics
rows.statement: Requires explicit tracking of translation loss to prevent downstream misinterpretation of completeness.

rows.anchor: M_{A,B} as a mapping between concepts. OrderStatus_A -> BillingStatus_B. But the mapping must describe the relationship: Equivalent, Broader, Narrower, Overlapping, Derived, Approximate
rows.statement: Defines semantic mapping between concepts requiring a typed relationship description.

rows.anchor: OrderStatus_A: Created, Confirmed, Shipped, Delivered, Cancelled. BillingStatus_B: Open, Paid, Overdue, Cancelled. There is no simple equality. Shipped might imply Open but not Shipped=Open
rows.statement: Worked order-status/billing-status example showing implication without equivalence.

rows.anchor: R_semantic in {SameMeaning, EquivalentUnderContext, Implies, CompatibleWith, MapsTo, Refines, Abstracts, ConflictsWith}
rows.statement: Defines an eight-value typed semantic-mapping relation taxonomy.

rows.anchor: A=>B, that does not mean A<=>B. This sounds elementary, but AI systems frequently collapse these distinctions. KnowledgeOS must not
rows.statement: Warns against collapsing implication into equivalence, a distinction AI systems frequently violate.

rows.anchor: Concept_B is more detailed than Concept_A. Then B may refine A. Approved may be refined into ApprovedByManager and ApprovedByBoard
rows.statement: Defines semantic refinement, worked with an Approved-refinement example.

rows.anchor: A may abstract several concepts B_1,B_2,B_3. OperationalFailure may abstract network failure; storage failure; process failure
rows.statement: Defines semantic abstraction as the converse of refinement, worked with an OperationalFailure example.

rows.anchor: B preceq A meaning B is more specific than A. This can form a semantic lattice or partial order. But we must not assume every domain naturally forms a complete lattice
rows.statement: Formalizes a cautious semantic partial-order/lattice structure, explicitly not assumed universal.

rows.anchor: A partial order requires reflexivity, antisymmetry, transitivity. Some domain relations satisfy these properties. Others do not. KnowledgeOS should represent the actual relation rather than force mathematical structure where none exists
rows.statement: Warns against forcing partial-order structure onto relations that do not actually satisfy its axioms.

rows.anchor: Contract(T). SourceContext, TargetContext, SourceConcept, TargetConcept, MappingRule, LossCharacteristics, Assumptions, ValidityPeriod
rows.statement: Defines a translation-contract schema with eight required fields.

rows.anchor: SalesEvidence -> SalesClaim -> Translation -> BillingClaim. Otherwise the target claim looks as though it originated directly from Billing
rows.statement: Requires translation provenance preserving the full source-to-target lineage.

rows.anchor: A translated claim should never masquerade as native evidence. TranslatedEvidence != NativeEvidence
rows.statement: States translated evidence must never be presented as native evidence.

rows.anchor: For E_A translated into E_B, we preserve Lineage(E_B) superset Lineage(E_A). This allows downstream users to inspect the original context
rows.statement: Formalizes evidence lineage preservation across translation.

rows.anchor: DDD commonly uses an Anti-Corruption Layer to protect one bounded context from another's model. KnowledgeOS should model this explicitly as ACL_{A->B}. The ACL performs Translation and SemanticProtection
rows.statement: Formalizes the DDD Anti-Corruption Layer as an explicit KnowledgeOS construct.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS should not say There is one universal Customer entity. Instead Customer_Sales and Customer_Billing remain context-owned. KnowledgeOS maintains the mappings between them
rows.statement: Major architectural warning against KnowledgeOS becoming a global/universal domain model.

rows.anchor: BC_A -> BC_B with a relationship: ContextMapping. upstream/downstream; conformist; partnership; customer/supplier; published language; anti-corruption layer. KnowledgeOS can represent these relationships without owning their business semantics
rows.statement: Defines context-map relationship types from DDD, represented without owning their business semantics.

rows.anchor: T_{A->B} != T_{B->A}. Even if both exist. This is another reason translation is not equality
rows.statement: States translation is generally directionally asymmetric.

rows.anchor: T_{B->C} circ T_{A->B} creates T_{A->C}. But semantic loss may accumulate
rows.statement: Formalizes translation composition and notes accumulating semantic loss.

rows.anchor: Loss(T_1)=L_1 and Loss(T_2)=L_2. Then Loss(T_2 circ T_1) may exceed either individually. composed mappings need explicit validation
rows.statement: Warns composed-translation loss can exceed either component's individual loss, requiring explicit validation.

rows.anchor: A->B->C. Each translation is individually valid. But information lost in A->B is needed in C. Expected: A->C must not automatically be considered valid
rows.statement: Runs a falsification test (PASS) showing individually-valid composed translations can still produce an invalid overall mapping due to accumulated information need.

experiment.hypothesis: A composed translation A->C is not automatically valid even if each component translation A->B and B->C is individually valid.
experiment.setup: A->B discards information needed downstream by C.
experiment.assumptions: n/a
experiment.inputs: n/a
experiment.method: apply translation composition and loss-tracking rules
experiment.result: A->C is correctly not automatically treated as valid
experiment.interpretation: confirms composed-loss accumulation must be explicitly checked, not assumed safe
experiment.limitations: illustrative, not executed
experiment.conclusion: PASS.

rows.anchor: source context guarantees Balance>=0. If translation preserves this property Invariant(T(x)). we should record it
rows.statement: Defines semantic-invariant preservation tracking across translation.

rows.anchor: I_A be a source invariant. I_B the corresponding target invariant. A translation is semantically safe if I_A(x) => I_B(T(x)) for the relevant domain
rows.statement: Formalizes translation correctness via invariant implication.

rows.anchor: Sometimes an invariant cannot be preserved. Then Preservation(I,T)=False. That does not necessarily make the translation invalid. It makes it unsuitable for uses requiring that invariant
rows.statement: Distinguishes invariant-preservation failure from outright translation invalidity, framing it as use-case unsuitability.

rows.anchor: Applicable(T,UseCase) must be evaluated. A translation can be valid for Reporting but invalid for OperationalDecision
rows.statement: Defines use-case-relative translation applicability.

rows.anchor: Mappings may themselves be uncertain. P(Equivalent(A,B))=0.8. Then the mapping is not confirmed. We need MappingStatus
rows.statement: Defines semantic-mapping confidence/status as distinct from a binary mapping decision.

rows.anchor: Candidate, Supported, Validated, Confirmed, Deprecated, Rejected. exact governance terminology should remain context-owned
rows.statement: Defines a six-value conceptual mapping-status taxonomy, terminology remaining context-owned.

rows.anchor: A mapping might be established by DomainExpert, FormalSpecification, ExistingIntegration, ObservedRuntimeBehavior, or AIInference. These have different epistemic strengths
rows.statement: Defines five mapping-evidence sources with differing epistemic strengths.

rows.anchor: an LLM proposes Customer_A~=Customer_B. That is useful candidate knowledge. But AIProposal != ConfirmedSemanticMapping. It must enter the same validation pipeline we established earlier
rows.statement: Distinguishes AI-proposed semantic mappings from confirmed mappings, requiring the standard validation pipeline.

rows.anchor: An AI system can invent relationships A->B that do not exist. KnowledgeOS therefore needs SemanticMappingValidation
rows.statement: Names 'semantic hallucination' as an AI failure mode requiring dedicated mapping validation.

rows.anchor: one expert says A->B. Another says A->C. Both cannot necessarily be simultaneously valid. KnowledgeOS should preserve MappingConflict. Not silently choose one
rows.statement: Requires preserving mapping conflicts rather than silently resolving them.

rows.anchor: A->B under Context_1 but A->C under Context_2. conflicts may disappear when context is modeled correctly
rows.statement: Worked example showing apparent mapping conflicts can dissolve once context is correctly modeled.

rows.anchor: Factual conflict: X=10 versus X=20. Semantic conflict: Two contexts use Approved with different meanings. The second is not necessarily contradiction
rows.statement: Distinguishes factual conflict from semantic conflict, a crucial distinction for correct contradiction detection.

rows.anchor: We should only infer A and not-A after establishing that Meaning(A_1)=Meaning(A_2) under the relevant context. This is a major safeguard
rows.statement: Requires semantic alignment as a precondition for inferring contradiction, a major safeguard.

rows.anchor: Approved_Manager and Approved_Board. Treating them as Approved may create a false contradiction
rows.statement: Worked example of false contradiction from collapsing context-specific terms.

rows.anchor: Two statements may use the same word Approved but mean different things. SameTerm does not imply SameProposition
rows.statement: Worked example of false agreement/polysemy: same term, different propositions.

rows.anchor: One term T may map to Meaning_1 and Meaning_2. KnowledgeOS must therefore model Term -> ContextualMeaning. Not Term -> GlobalMeaning
rows.statement: Defines polysemy handling via contextual, not global, term-to-meaning mapping.

rows.anchor: This is precisely why DDD uses bounded-context-specific Ubiquitous Language. KnowledgeOS should preserve UL_BC1 and UL_BC2 rather than flattening them
rows.statement: Requires preserving per-bounded-context Ubiquitous Language rather than flattening it into one vocabulary.

rows.anchor: Dictionary_{A->B}. But this is more than a word dictionary. It should encode SemanticTransformation
rows.statement: Defines a translation dictionary as encoding full semantic transformation, not mere word substitution.

rows.anchor: Status_A={Draft,Approved,Rejected} and Status_B={Open,Closed}. Draft->Open, Approved->Open, Rejected->Closed. But this is many-to-one. Therefore T is lossy
rows.statement: Worked many-to-one status-mapping example demonstrating lossiness.

rows.anchor: If H(A)>H(B), then a deterministic mapping A->B may reduce distinguishability. The target cannot reconstruct all source states. This provides a mathematical interpretation of semantic loss
rows.statement: Provides an entropy-based mathematical interpretation of semantic loss under deterministic mapping.

rows.anchor: we should not equate SemanticInformation with Shannon entropy universally ... H(A)>H(B) is evidence of possible information loss, not proof of semantic invalidity
rows.statement: Distinguishes semantic information from Shannon entropy, limiting the entropy interpretation to evidentiary, not conclusive, status.

rows.anchor: T:A->B is an abstraction if multiple source states map to one target state. T(a_1)=T(a_2) while a_1 != a_2. This is legitimate if the distinction is irrelevant to the target use case
rows.statement: Defines translation-as-abstraction as legitimate when the collapsed distinction is use-case-irrelevant.

rows.anchor: Safe(T,U) depends on use case U. If U needs the distinction between a_1 and a_2, then the abstraction is unsafe
rows.statement: Defines abstraction safety as use-case-relative.

rows.anchor: Every cross-context mapping should ideally carry Purpose. Purpose=Reporting versus Purpose=OperationalExecution
rows.statement: Requires purpose-tagging of cross-context mappings.

rows.anchor: A translation may be FitForReporting=True but FitForDecision=False. This is another form of typed epistemic safety
rows.statement: Defines fitness-for-purpose typing of translations as an instance of typed epistemic safety.

rows.anchor: Contract(T)=(Preconditions,Postconditions,Invariants,Loss,Applicability). Then translation becomes a verifiable operation
rows.statement: Formalizes translation as a verifiable contract-bearing operation.

rows.anchor: Environment=Production. or Currency=EUR. If preconditions fail, T must not execute silently
rows.statement: Requires translation preconditions to gate execution rather than silently proceeding.

rows.anchor: T(A) produces B. The contract may require Invariant_B(B)=True
rows.statement: Defines translation postconditions as target-invariant requirements.

rows.anchor: Success, PartialSuccess, LossySuccess, Ambiguous, Invalid, Rejected. Again, do not collapse these into Success/Failure
rows.statement: Defines a six-value non-binary translation-result taxonomy.

rows.anchor: T^(1) may differ from T^(2). A claim translated under T^(1) must retain that mapping version
rows.statement: Requires translation-version tracking on translated claims.

rows.anchor: Meaning_A(t_1) != Meaning_A(t_2). Then an old mapping may become invalid. SemanticDrift. This extends Step 36's drift concept
rows.statement: Defines semantic drift as an extension of Step 36's drift taxonomy.

rows.anchor: A mapping can have ValidFrom and ValidUntil. Then Applicable(T,t) can be evaluated
rows.statement: Defines a mapping validity interval for time-indexed applicability.

rows.anchor: a decision in 2025 used T^(1). In 2026 T^(2) replaces it. We must still be able to reconstruct Decision_2025 using T^(1). This connects directly to temporal knowledge
rows.statement: Requires historical reconstruction of past decisions using the mapping version in force at the time.

rows.anchor: a cross-context claim should have lineage SourceClaim -> MappingVersion -> TranslatedClaim -> Decision. This is essential for auditability
rows.statement: Formalizes translation lineage as essential for auditability.

rows.anchor: Experiments 2-7: mapping discards source information->Lossy=True PASS; mapping valid for reporting but invalid for operational decisions->use-case-specific applicability PASS; translation performed under T_1 later deprecated->historical claim traceable to T_1 PASS; AI proposes a semantic mapping->ca
rows.statement: Runs falsification tests 2-7 (all PASS): lossy mappings are correctly flagged; use-case-specific applicability is respected; deprecated mapping versions remain traceable on historical claims; AI-proposed mappings remain candidates rather than auto-confirmed; apparent cross-context contradictions dissolve correctly under semantic mapping without deleting source claims; and unsatisfied preconditions correctly reject/invalidate a translation.

experiment.hypothesis: The translation model correctly handles lossiness flagging, use-case applicability, version traceability, AI-proposal status, false-contradiction dissolution, and precondition gating.
experiment.setup: Six scenarios each isolating one property.
experiment.assumptions: n/a
experiment.inputs: n/a
experiment.method: apply the loss/applicability/versioning/AI-status/semantic-conflict/precondition rules to each scenario
experiment.result: all six produce the theoretically expected outcome
experiment.interpretation: confirms these six translation-model properties
experiment.limitations: illustrative, not executed
experiment.conclusion: All six tests PASS.

rows.anchor: Experiments 8-12: translation maps several source states into one target state->information-loss metadata preserved PASS; two mappings valid in different contexts->no forced global conflict PASS; mapping changes after semantic drift->old knowledge retains historical mapping, new knowledge uses new m
rows.statement: Runs falsification tests 8-12 (all PASS): many-to-one mappings preserve loss metadata; context-local mapping validity avoids forced global conflict; semantic drift correctly preserves historical mapping alongside the new one; unpreservable invariants are explicitly declared lost; and lossy-mapping-discarded information correctly fails to satisfy a downstream decision's evidence requirement.

experiment.hypothesis: The translation model correctly handles many-to-one loss metadata, context-local validity, drift-aware historical preservation, invariant-loss declaration, and evidence-sufficiency failure from lossy translation.
experiment.setup: Five scenarios each isolating one property.
experiment.assumptions: n/a
experiment.inputs: n/a
experiment.method: apply the abstraction/context-validity/drift/invariant/evidence-sufficiency rules to each scenario
experiment.result: all five produce the theoretically expected outcome
experiment.interpretation: confirms these five final translation-model properties
experiment.limitations: illustrative, not executed
experiment.conclusion: All five tests PASS.

rows.anchor: STEP 39 — PASS. We have now established a mathematically disciplined way to move knowledge between bounded contexts without pretending that the contexts share one universal domain model
rows.statement: Step 39 self-verdict: PASS.

rows.anchor: Same referent != Same domain concept ... Knowledge sharing != Knowledge merging ... Translation != Identity ... Translated evidence must preserve its origin ... Semantic loss must be explicit ... A mapping is valid only relative to a context and purpose ... Semantic equivalence must be established,
rows.statement: States eight major boxed Step 39 principles: same referent does not imply same concept; knowledge sharing does not imply merging; translation does not imply identity; translated evidence must preserve origin; semantic loss must be explicit; mappings are valid only relative to context and purpose; semantic equivalence must be established rather than assumed from lexical similarity; and bounded contexts remain autonomous.

rows.anchor: REAL WORLD -> MULTIPLE CONTEXTS (BC-A, BC-B, BC-C with Local Meaning) -> Context Maps / Semantic Maps -> Translation Contracts (Lossless/Lossy) -> SHARED KNOWLEDGE (Provenance retained) -> DECISION. BC_A != BC_B != BC_C even though knowledge can flow between them
rows.statement: Presents an updated multi-context architecture diagram preserving context autonomy while allowing knowledge flow.

rows.anchor: Identity transformation: Reference->Entity. Semantic transformation: Concept_A->Concept_B. Epistemic transformation: Evidence->Claim->Model. Decision transformation: Knowledge->Action. These should never be collapsed into one generic Transform()
rows.statement: Distinguishes four transformation kinds that must never be collapsed into one generic transform operation.

rows.anchor: An AI agent may encounter Approved and assume it has one universal meaning. KnowledgeOS should instead require Approved(Context=C) ... This dramatically reduces semantic hallucination
rows.statement: Argues context-tagged terms dramatically reduce AI semantic hallucination compared to assumed-universal meaning.

rows.anchor: KOS = {(K_C,G_C,T_C)}_{C in Contexts} where K_C=knowledge within context C, G_C=contextual semantics/dependencies, T_C=translation mappings ... much closer to a genuine DDD architecture than a monolithic ontology
rows.statement: Formally defines KnowledgeOS as a multi-context epistemic system, called a deeper result closer to genuine DDD architecture.

rows.anchor: Both refer to the same real-world entity but define different concepts, attributes, lifecycle rules, and invariants. How should knowledge cross the boundary? ... How can knowledge be transferred across bounded contexts without destroying semantic integrity? That is more than entity resolution. It is
rows.statement: Closes by posing the cross-bounded-context knowledge-transfer question, transitioning to Step 39 (Bounded-Context Translation, Semantic Mapping, Conceptual Alignment and Knowledge Interoperability), duplicating content already extracted from S0932, previewing translation mappings, semantic invariants, anti-corruption boundaries, lossless/lossy translation, mapping uncertainty, semantic drift, and cross-context contradiction under the principle Knowledge can be shared without concepts being identical.

sources.note: The 20260830_1918 mandate's canonical, executable Knowledge State model K=(Assertions,Relations), empirically validated against the running EKP (which only reconstructs 4/9 theory items) and against a component-removal minimality audit; introduces the symmetric related_to relation family (R_rel) discovered from the implementation rather than derived in advance.

rows.anchor: The running EKP was parsed into (𝒜, ℛ): |𝒜| = 37, |ℛ| = 51, relation types related_to (46), derived_from (2), requires (3).
rows.statement: The running Engineering Knowledge Platform was parsed directly into the theory's (Assertions,Relations) shape: 37 assertions, 51 relations, with relation types related_to (46), derived_from (2), requires (3); EKP's own assertion type is (knowledge_id, title, bounded_context, status, authority, knowledge_type, owner).

experiment.hypothesis: the running EKP instantiates the theory's K=(A,R) shape
experiment.setup: parse the EKP's knowledge documents into (A,R)
experiment.assumptions: EKP documents map to assertions, EKP typed edges map to relations
experiment.inputs: EKP's governed knowledge documents and edges
experiment.method: direct parse/count
experiment.result: |A|=37, |R|=51, three relation types counted
experiment.interpretation: the EKP does instantiate the (set,relations) SHAPE
experiment.limitations: shape match only; field-level content differs, see next contribution
experiment.conclusion: EXECUTED

rows.anchor: id YES ... c YES ... P structured NO — title is prose ... e evidence NO ... t temporal validity NO — the schema has no temporal field at all ... Π provenance NO — authority is a trust rank, not an origin
rows.statement: Field-by-field comparison of the theory's Assertion=(id,P,e,c,t,Pi) against the EKP's actual schema: id and c (context) are present (knowledge_id, bounded_context), but P is unstructured prose (title), and e (evidence), t (temporal validity), and Pi (provenance) are entirely absent from the EKP schema.

rows.anchor: VERDICT: the EKP's (𝒜,ℛ) is E — a bounded-context-specific model — and B — a representation. It is NOT C (a projection of the theory's K), because a projection cannot invent the fields it lacks. ... Therefore: ontology ≠ implementation representation.
rows.statement: Central §5 verdict: the EKP's (A,R) is a bounded-context-specific model (category E) and a representation (category B), NOT a projection of the theory's K (category C), since a projection cannot invent fields it lacks; it is a different K over a different, non-epistemic assertion type (governed documents, not epistemic assertions); the mandate's central warning that ontology != implementation representation is thereby empirically demonstrated, not merely avoided — the two K's share shape (identified items + typed relations) but differ in carrier.

rows.anchor: 4 of 9 reconstructible. The EKP is an adequate governance-document store and an inadequate epistemic store — and it was never built to be the latter.
rows.statement: Reconstructibility audit: of §5's nine listed items, only context, supersession, identity, and governance boundaries are reconstructible from the EKP (4 of 9); epistemic qualification, evidence references, temporal validity, contradiction, and provenance are not — the EKP is an adequate governance-document store and an inadequate epistemic store, and was never built to be the latter.

rows.statement: Structural (by-construction) explanation for why congruence held in every test: T's derived signature K x Op x Policy x Authority -harpoon-> K x Outcome does not include History in its domain, so T cannot depend on it — a function cannot depend on an argument it does not receive. rows.anchor: A2 is the one that could fail. Any future operation reading insertion order — "the first assertion wins", "the most recently added is authoritative" — breaks congruence immediately. That is a design constraint the theory now states explicitly rather than assumes silently.
rows.statement: Explicit forward-looking design constraint: assumption A2 (no operation consults insertion order) is violable by future design — any future operation implementing 'first assertion wins' or 'most recently added is authoritative' semantics would break congruence immediately; the theory now states this as an explicit constraint rather than a silent assumption.

rows.anchor: SUFFICIENT UNDER ASSUMPTIONS. Not sufficient unqualified: the assumptions are real and A2 is violable by future design. Not insufficient: no counterexample exists and none can, given A1. Not unknown: the test was constructed correctly and executed.
rows.statement: Final classification: the Knowledge-State/History sufficiency question is SUFFICIENT UNDER ASSUMPTIONS — deliberately neither 'sufficient unqualified' (the assumptions A1/A2 are real and A2 is violable), nor 'insufficient' (no counterexample exists, and none can given A1), nor 'unknown' (the test was validly constructed and executed).

rows.anchor: Knowledge State is sufficient for FUTURE COMPUTATION. It is NOT sufficient for GOVERNANCE AUDIT. ... Who asserted this, and when? NO ... Was every admission properly authorised? NO — GovernanceValid(K,Γ) needs History ... What did we believe last March? NO — needs History
rows.statement: The state/history sufficiency boundary is drawn precisely: K alone answers what is currently held, what follows from an operation (congruence), whether structural/semantic invariants hold, and current epistemic status (recomputable from e); K alone CANNOT answer who asserted something and when, whether every admission was properly authorised (GovernanceValid(K,Gamma) needs History), or what was believed at a past point in time (needs History or a bitemporal interpretation of t).

rows.anchor: K answers what is known. History answers how it came to be known and by whom. Neither reduces to the other, and T needs only the first.
rows.statement: Governing principle stated as the resolution of the state/history boundary the programme has circled since the executed History(K)!=K counterexample: K answers what is known; History answers how it came to be known and by whom; neither reduces to the other, and the transformation function T needs only K.

rows.anchor: The objective is NOT to produce the most elegant theory. If these disagree, preserve the disagreement and investigate
rows.statement: States the mandate's most important methodological rule: the goal is a theory that survives five simultaneous tests (historical traceability, mathematical scrutiny, executable computation, empirical falsification, DDD semantic consistency) — when these disagree, the disagreement must be preserved and investigated, never silently repaired away to make the pieces fit.

rows.anchor: 'Mandatory operations' O. The corpus (Step 266) never closes this set. We therefore define TWO defensible closures and show the answer depends on it. OPS_MINIMAL = {query, explain} OPS_FULL = {query, explain, withdraw, contest}
rows.statement: Because Step 266 never closes the mandatory-operation set, the kernel implements two distinct, both-defensible operation-set closures (OPS_MINIMAL: query+explain; OPS_FULL: query+explain+withdraw+contest) explicitly in order to demonstrate, executably, that downstream answers about K's sufficiency/minimality depend on which operation-set closure is chosen — a runnable confirmation of the theory-evolution-map's EV-E1 finding that the transformation/operation algebra was never actually enumerated.

experiment.hypothesis: the mandatory operation set materially affects conclusions about K's adequacy

rows.statement: Four explicit, corpus-cited hypotheses are set up for direct executable testing: H1 (content-only state abstraction is insufficient), H2 (placing provenance inside the assertion repairs H1), H3 (the terminal K=(A,R) with in-assertion provenance is a sufficient history abstraction), and H4 (this session's own claim that H3's truth is undetermined because it depends on the never-closed mandatory operation set) — using the Step 259/260 sufficiency-plus-congruence criterion as the formal test.

experiment.hypothesis: H1: a content-only Knowledge-State abstraction is sufficient for the mandatory operations

But a plausible governance operation this session constructs directly from the corpus's own material -- escalate any assertion that has EVER been contested, regardless of current state -- is explicitly not computable from K=(A,R) alone, since it requires the full history; run directly against the two raw histories, ever_contested(H_calm,P)=False while ever_contested(H_stormy,P)=True, despite both replaying to the same K.

experiment.hypothesis: H3: K=(A,R) is a sufficient abstraction of history for all mandatory KnowledgeOS operations
experiment.setup: H_calm (assert once) and H_stormy (assert, contradicting assertion appears, is related as contradicting, then withdrawn) both replay to a structurally identical K

experiment.method: replay both histories to K; check structural equality; test both operation-set closures for a distinguishing operation; then construct and test an additional plausible operation (ever_contested) directly against the histories
experiment.result: the two K's are structurally identical and indistinguishable under either coded operation set, but ever_contested(H_calm)=False vs ever_contested(H_stormy)=True and this predicate is not computable from K=(A,R) at all
experiment.interpretation: whether K=(A,R) is sufficient depends entirely on whether the mandatory operation set includes history-sensitive predicates like ever_contested
experiment.limitations: ever_contested is a constructed, not corpus-mandated, operation, though motivated by plausible governance material
experiment.conclusion: H3 UNDECIDED

rationale_evidence.statement: Central §5 verdict: the EKP's (A,R) is a bounded-context-specific model (category E) and a representation (category B), NOT a projection of the theory's K (category C), since a projection cannot invent fields it lacks; it is a different K over a different, non-epistemic assertion type (governed documents, not epistemic assertions); the mandate's central warning that ontology != implementation representation is thereby empirically demonstrated, not merely avoided — the two K's share shape (identified items + typed relations) but differ in carrier.

rationale_evidence.anchor: a working knowledge platform was built without temporal validity, evidence, provenance or epistemic status. The theory must explain that omission, not ignore it. ... EKP's assertions are documents under governance ... the theory's assertions are claims under evidence, for which they do not [suffice]
rationale_evidence.statement: Most instructive fact of the artifact: a real working knowledge platform operates without temporal validity, evidence, provenance, or epistemic status fields, because its assertions are 'documents under governance' (for which lifecycle and authority suffice), whereas the theory's assertions are 'claims under evidence' (for which they do not) — the theory is obligated to explain this omission rather than dismiss it.

rationale_evidence.anchor: T's derived signature is 𝕂 × Op × Policy × Authority ⇀ 𝕂 × Outcome. History is not in its domain. A function cannot depend on an argument it does not receive. Congruence therefore holds by construction, under exactly two assumptions: A1 · T reads only K, Policy, Authority — PROVEN ... A2 · no operat
rationale_evidence.statement: Structural (by-construction) explanation for why congruence held in every test: T's derived signature K x Op x Policy x Authority -harpoon-> K x Outcome does not include History in its domain, so T cannot depend on it — a function cannot depend on an argument it does not receive. This holds under exactly two assumptions: A1 (T reads only K, Policy, Authority — PROVEN by elimination of actor/time/evidence/context during signature derivation) and A2 (no operation consults order-of-arrival — HOLDS for the twelve derived operations because A and R are sets, making order structurally unobservable).

rationale_evidence.anchor: 9 | Contradiction is ℛ-relative and context-sensitive — three cases, three correct answers. contradicts(A1,A2)=False because supersession explains it; contradicts(A1,A3)=False because the contexts differ (230.9)
rationale_evidence.statement: Line 9 demonstrates contradiction is relation-relative (R-relative) and context-sensitive by producing three different correct answers for three assertion pairs: contradicts(A1,A2)=False because the supersedes relation explains the difference, contradicts(A1,A4)=True as an unexplained genuine contradiction, and contradicts(A1,A3)=False because A1 and A3 differ in context (citing step 230.9's context-sensitivity finding).

rationale_evidence.statement: Eight theory predicates are ENGINEERINGALLY VERIFIED against the real EKP with a named enforcing mechanism and executable test each: unique identity (knowledge_id_unique+pattern, 37 docs 0 errors), no dangling endpoints (relationship_targets_exist, covering both .md and package .yaml), R being typed (knowledge-relationships.yaml + relationship_keys_valid), supersession-as-relation-not-deletion (supersedes/superseded_by + status:superseded, old retained), Gamma having a controlled vocabulary (authorities.yaml, 5 ranked values, enum_values_valid), Sigma-perp-Gamma orthogonality (authorities.yaml's explicit 'INDEPENDENT of status' statement plus a worked cross-quadrant example, both enums enforced separately — called the strongest result in the whole programme), context scoping (bounded_context error-level plus boundary_consistency warning), and determinism of derivation (knowledge-graph.php executed twice, byte-identical, 39 nodes/70 edges).

rationale_evidence.anchor: Context c has already been shown to be necessary at assertion level ... the executed removal analysis explicitly reports context as irrecoverable. But that does not mean context should be inserted into P. ... Otherwise we risk destroying the distinction between proposition and assertion.
rationale_evidence.statement: Context must not leak into the Proposition type: although context c is independently necessary at the Assertion level (an executed removal test found it irrecoverable), inserting it into P would collapse the proposition/assertion distinction — P remains the semantic proposition, c remains the situational assertion context.

rationale_evidence.anchor: e is outside P. The executed removal test found that evidence cannot be derived from proposition content. Therefore P ≠ (P,e). Evidence is associated with the assertion, not intrinsic to proposition identity. This preserves Same(P) while allowing DifferentEvidence(A1,A2).
rationale_evidence.statement: Evidence must not leak into the Proposition type: an executed removal test found evidence cannot be derived from proposition content, so P is not (P,e) — evidence attaches to the assertion, preserving that the same proposition can appear with different evidence across different assertions.

rationale_evidence.anchor: t belongs to Assertion. The executed counterexample found that one proposition may have two validity intervals, forcing the system to wrap propositions in assertions. Therefore P must not carry assertion-specific validity ... Temporal multiplicity is an assertion phenomenon, not necessarily a propos
rationale_evidence.statement: Major result: temporal validity t must not leak into P, because an executed counterexample found a single proposition can have two distinct validity intervals (requiring the system to wrap propositions in separate assertions to represent both) — temporal multiplicity is an assertion-level phenomenon, not a proposition-identity phenomenon.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Note the pleasing duality with K: (𝕂, merge, ∅) is a join-semilattice — adding knowledge only grows the state. (Policy, ∧) is a meet-semilattice — adding policy only shrinks admissibility. Knowledge accumulates; permission contracts. Neither is an aesthetic choice; both were executed.
rationale_evidence.statement: A structural duality is identified between the two central algebraic objects of the theory: (K, merge, empty) is a join-semilattice (knowledge only accumulates/grows), while (Policy, AND) is a meet-semilattice (permission only contracts) — 'knowledge accumulates; permission contracts', explicitly noted as an executed structural finding, not an aesthetic observation.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Π=History(T)? No — not universally. The base-case counterexample disproves this. ... REFUTED as a universal identity. But a weaker statement survives: History(T) can reconstruct internal transformation lineage. It cannot replace external provenance. ... external audit alone is insufficient unless K
rationale_evidence.statement: Candidates B, C, and D are each addressed: Candidate B (Pi=History(T)) is REFUTED as a universal identity by the base-case counterexample, though History(T) can still reconstruct internal transformation lineage; Candidate C (external-audit-only) is found insufficient alone because Merge could destroy the provenance association unless K itself carries a stable resolvable reference, pushing back toward pi in K; Candidate D (provenance-as-context) is refuted because context ('under what circumstances does this apply') and provenance ('where did this originate') answer different questions and are already kept as distinct fields.

rows.statement: Draws on Brahmagupta's fortune/debt framing of signed quantities (not the Atharva Veda itself) to establish that a negative quantity is a signed deviation relative to a reference, not mere absence, formalizing Knowledge = Reference + Deviation via K=B+Delta_B(K) with excess/exact-match/deficiency corresponding to Delta_B(K) being positive/zero/negative.

rows.anchor: Delta_{T,Pi}(x;D) in C where C is a contribution space. Only later do we ask whether C=R or some ordered group, lattice, vector space, partially ordered set, etc. That is the mathematician's safer route.
rows.statement: Generalizes the positive/zero/negative contribution notion to an abstract contribution space C (Delta_{T,Pi}(x;D) in C), deferring the question of whether C is the reals or some ordered group, lattice, vector space, or poset until later, as the mathematically safer route.

rows.anchor: Supporting evidence: e -> +p. Contradictory evidence: e -> -p. Irrelevant evidence: e -> 0. Undetermined: e -> ?. Notice that 0 != negative and negative != false. This is absolutely critical.
rows.statement: Distinguishes four fundamentally different evidence-to-proposition situations (supporting, contradictory, irrelevant, undetermined), explicitly flagging as absolutely critical that zero contribution is not negative contribution, and negative contribution is not falsity.

rows.anchor: 'The database contains no record supporting proposition p.' That may be negative evidence. But it does not automatically mean not-p. negative contribution != false proposition. Polarity of contribution != truth value. truth != evidence polarity.
rows.statement: Argues that negative evidence (e.g. absence of a supporting record) does not automatically mean the proposition is false, establishing the DDD-style separations Polarity-of-contribution != truth-value and truth != evidence-polarity.

rows.anchor: Truth=true, Evidence contribution=negative, Decision utility=negative, Knowledge relevance=zero. There is no contradiction. a true fact can be irrelevant to the current question. A true fact can also be evidence against a particular hypothesis. And a true fact can have negative practical utility. we
rows.statement: Constructs a non-contradictory example (a true fact with negative evidence contribution, negative decision utility, and zero knowledge relevance simultaneously) to argue against ever computing a single universal sign(K) for a knowledge item, requiring instead a fully typed Sign_{Q,C,T,Pi}(x) relative to question, contract, transformation, and observable.

rows.anchor: A. Debt/deficit: Delta<0. B. Opposition: Oppose(x,Q) rather than simply x=0. C. Removal: E_x(D) followed by testing whether the relevant observable changes -- our Zero territory. D. Purification/transformation: P:D->D' such that some undesirable property decreases while designated invariants remain
rows.statement: Extracts four structural ideas from the Atharva Veda (not 'negative numbers'): debt/deficit as Delta<0, opposition as a distinct Oppose(x,Q) predicate rather than x=0, removal as E_x(D) tested for observable change (the existing Zero territory), and purification/transformation as P:D->D' decreasing an undesirable property while preserving designated invariants.

rows.anchor: So I would NOT define Knowledge Negative as -Knowledge. We should not say -K until we have discovered an actual additive/invertible structure on knowledge states. Instead: Neg_{T,Pi,Q}(x;D) could initially mean: x has an adverse or opposing contribution to the specified observable under the specifie
rows.statement: Refuses to define Knowledge Negative as -Knowledge until an actual additive/invertible structure on knowledge states is discovered, defining instead the safer relational predicate Neg_{T,Pi,Q}(x;D): x has an adverse or opposing contribution to the specified observable under the specified transformation and inquiry.
