Defines a six-field verification tuple V_i=(Invariant, Owner, EnforcementMechanism, MonitoringMechanism, Test, FailureBehavior) for every invariant, giving the bridge Theory -> Architecture -> Implementation -> Evidence; states the first verification rule 'no claim of architectural compliance without identifiable evidence', naming acceptable evidence types (code, schema, state machine, automated test, configuration, event, immutable record, architecture decision, runtime observation) and explicitly excluding a bare documentation statement as sufficient evidence for an executable property.

rows.anchor: 210.25 The assurance matrix ... I1 Identity!=State ... I15 No semantic strengthening ... This is now a real architecture assurance matrix, rather than merely a list of principles.
rows.statement: Consolidates Step 209's derived invariants into a numbered, owner-and-verification-assigned assurance matrix of 15 invariants: I1 Identity!=State (Domain owner, identity transition test); I2 historical version preserved (Persistence/Domain, version reconstruction); I3 provenance preserved (Knowledge infrastructure, lineage traversal); I4 epistemic status preserved (Assessment/Contracts, semantic contract test); I5 Unknown!=False (Assessment, negative inference test); I6 uncertainty preserved (Assessment/Contracts, payload/semantic test); I7 model version preserved (Assessment, reproducibility test); I8 Inference!=Authority (Governance, privilege-path test); I9 Decision!=Execution (Decision/Execution, failure simulation); I10 Execution!=Outcome (Execution/Observation, outcome verification); I11 contradiction preserved (Knowledge, conflict test); I12 temporal validity preserved (Governance, historical replay); I13 illegal transitions rejected (Aggregate, state-machine test); I14 preconditions/postconditions (Aggregate, invariant test); I15 no semantic strengthening (Contracts, transformation test) -- judged a real architecture assurance matrix rather than merely a list of principles.

lineage_claims.quote: This is now a real architecture assurance matrix, rather than merely a list of principles.

rows.anchor: 210.26 But there is a deeper issue ... Who verifies the verifier? ... a test provides evidence. It does not necessarily provide a mathematical proof. ... 210.27 Three assurance levels ... Documentation < ExecutableEvidence < FormalProof ... This does not mean every property needs formal proof.
rows.statement: Poses 'who verifies the verifier?', distinguishing TestEvidence (a passing test provides evidence about tested conditions) from FormalProof (a proof/model-checking/static-verification result holding within a defined formal model), and establishes three assurance levels in strictly increasing strength: Level 1 Documentation assurance (a claim exists in architecture documentation), Level 2 Executable assurance (an automated test demonstrates the property under tested conditions), Level 3 Formal assurance (proof/model checking/static verification establishes the property within a formal model) -- boxed Documentation < ExecutableEvidence < FormalProof, while explicitly not requiring every property to reach formal proof.

rows.anchor: 210.28 Risk-based assurance ... Critical(I) => HigherAssurance(I). ... 210.29 Assurance confidence ... Assurance(I)=f(Evidence,Coverage,Independence,Repeatability,Criticality). We should not yet turn this into a numerical score. A fake precision such as Assurance=97.3% would be misleading unless we have a justified statistical model. ... 210.30 Evidence hierarchy E1...E5.
rows.statement: Proposes risk-based assurance: critical invariants (e.g. preventing UnauthorizedExecution) deserve stronger assurance than low-risk ones (e.g. PayloadFormatting), where statistical risk thinking meets architecture governance. Defines a conceptual (deliberately non-numericized) assurance-confidence function Assurance(I) = f(Evidence, Coverage, Independence, Repeatability, Criticality), explicitly refusing to convert it into a numeric score, warning a fake-precision value like 'Assurance=97.3%' would be misleading absent a justified statistical model. Ranks a five-level evidence hierarchy: documentation, manual inspection, automated test, property-based test, formal verification.
missing: a justified statistical model that would license numericizing the assurance function

rows.anchor: 210.32 State-space thinking ... An invariant I is globally valid if for-all s in S_reachable: I(s)=True. This is the mathematically stronger formulation. The challenge is determining S_reachable. ... 210.34 This changes our definition of architecture ... Architecture = Structure + Semantics + State + Constraints + Contracts + Invariants + Evidence.
rows.statement: Reframes invariant verification as a state-space reachability problem, the mathematically stronger formulation: an invariant I is globally valid only if it holds for all states s in the reachable set S_reachable (given initial state s0 and transitions T), not merely for a finite set of tested cases -- explicitly naming the determination of S_reachable as the open challenge. Uses this to redefine Architecture itself: no longer merely Components+Interfaces, but Structure + Semantics + State + Constraints + Contracts + Invariants + Evidence, judged a much more complete definition for KnowledgeOS.
missing: a constructed characterization of S_reachable

rows.anchor: 210.36 AI's proper role ... AI can help: Discover, Classify, Suggest, Explain, Generate but deterministic mechanisms should establish critical invariants wherever feasible. AI may assist assurance; AI should not be the sole source of assurance.
rows.statement: Bounds AI's proper role within the assurance architecture: AI can assist with discovery, classification, suggestion, explanation, and generation, but deterministic mechanisms should establish critical invariants wherever feasible, boxed 'AI may assist assurance; AI should not be the sole source of assurance.' Connects the Gita-Chapter-4 lens operationally: the question of what should be done must not be answered merely by what a model predicts, but must pass through the full Prediction -> Assessment -> Governance -> Decision -> Action chain, each transition carrying its own assurance boundary.

rows.anchor: 210.38 The "new state does not know old state" insight ... CurrentState not-superset-or-equal CompleteHistory necessarily. But the architecture should preserve historical lineage when required: CurrentState -> HistoryReference. ... 210.39 The important distinction ... distinguish Memory from Identity and History.
rows.statement: Makes the recurring 'new state does not know old state' insight testable: CurrentState is not required to be a superset of CompleteHistory, but the architecture must preserve a HistoryReference from CurrentState when required -- judged a better architectural interpretation than requiring every object to carry its entire past internally. Distinguishes Memory from Identity from History, noting a system may preserve history externally through immutable records, event logs, versioned artifacts, or provenance structures, so the current domain object need not carry all history internally -- called a powerful DDD consequence.

rows.anchor: Step 210 Verdict DDD VERY STRONG, Mathematics VERY STRONG, Governance VERY STRONG, AI VERY STRONG ... Step 211 -- The Architecture Assurance Graph ... AAG=(Components,Contracts,Invariants,Evidence,Dependencies) ... Which invariants currently have NO owner or enforcement mechanism? Those are the architecture assurance gaps.
rows.statement: Closes Step 210 with the strongest verdict cluster yet -- DDD, Mathematics, Governance, and AI all rated VERY STRONG, Statistics STRONG, and the Gita Chapters 1-4 lens rated 'COHERENT AND OPERATIONAL' -- and summarizes the achieved pipeline as Invariant -> Owner -> Enforcement -> Evidence -> Test -> Assurance. Opens Step 211 (The Architecture Assurance Graph), proposing AAG = (Components, Contracts, Invariants, Evidence, Dependencies) to answer, for every critical invariant, which component enforces it, which contract carries it, which test proves it, and what happens if it fails -- explicitly targeting the discovery of invariants with no owner or enforcement mechanism at all, named 'architecture assurance gaps', framed as the point where the programme shifts from designing an ideal KnowledgeOS to measuring the distance between the derived architecture and the actual software.

lineage_claims.quote: Which invariants currently have NO owner or enforcement mechanism? Those are the architecture assurance gaps.

rows.anchor: Headlines - the most severe defects found in the corpus so far: 1. Step-048's induction obligations are STATED and NEVER DISCHARGED for any of I1-I20, and ReachableStates is never characterised - yet the file issues STEP 48 - PASS, which its own 48.33 (Specification != Proof) forbids.
rows.statement: Confirms, with full section-level detail, that step-048 states two proof obligations for its 20 global invariants -- the preservation obligation I(s) and ValidTransition(s,s') implies I(s'), and the initial-state obligation I(S_0)=True -- and discharges neither for a single one of I1-I20 anywhere in the file: no base case is exhibited, no transition-by-transition preservation argument is given, and ValidTransition/T is never enumerated; ReachableStates is likewise never characterized (no finite abstraction is ever exhibited despite being proposed). Despite this, the file issues 'STEP 48 -- PASS', a move its own stated rule (Specification != Proof) explicitly forbids -- identified as the single largest gap between claim strength and evidence in the whole batch. Also finds two incompatible definitions of 'Correctness' within the same file (a 6-element set versus a 5-fold intersection over a different index, neither matching the file's own headline KOSCorrect formula) and a double meaning of the symbol I_i (the i-th global invariant versus the invariant of a specific bounded context) within one document.
missing: a discharged base case and preservation proof for any I_i
a characterization of ReachableStates
a resolution between the two incompatible Correctness definitions

lineage_claims.quote: section48.75's KOSCorrect ... section48.89's boxed STEP 48 -- PASS follows [despite] section48.37's induction [being] an open conditional

rows.anchor: 2. Step-051 silently substitutes 5 of the 20 invariants (5 dropped, 5 added, cardinality held at 20, masking a 25-percent change) under an explicit promise to test I_1...I_20. The dropped set includes I7 Execute(d) => Admissible(d) - the invariant 48.18 calls "one of the most important system invariants".
rows.statement: Confirms step-051 drops five of step-048's 20 invariants without notice (I4 Identity integrity, I7 Decision integrity/Execute-implies-Admissible, I9 Safety integrity, I17 Independent validation, I20 Causal-model integrity) and adds five others (Model invalidation, Knowledge demotion, Computational uncertainty, Action-outcome linkage, Governance compliance), holding cardinality at exactly 20 -- masking a 25% substitution of content behind an unchanged count. Identifies the dropped I7 as the most consequential loss: it is precisely the invariant step-048 itself calls 'one of the most important system invariants' and the one binding execution to the full admissibility conjunction; the reference machine's substitute (authorization only) is strictly weaker, so the executable reference model as specified never tests admissibility at all, despite step-050's closing text explicitly promising to test I_1 through I_20.
missing: I7 (Execute implies Admissible) tested against the reference machine

lineage_claims.target: step-048's I1-I20 invariant set and the promise to test it
lineage_claims.quote: The most important dropped invariant, I7, is precisely the one binding execution to the full admissibility conjunction... INV-6 (authorization only) is strictly weaker, so the reference machine as specified does not test admissibility at all.

rows.anchor: STEP 041 ... FIRST INVALID INFERENCE: section41.8 -- "An average gives: 0.693" from {0.99,0.99,0.10} ... conflating a mean of assurance scores with a safety probability, which is exactly the category error the section is warning against, committed in the act of warning.
rows.statement: Step-041 (Epistemic Sufficiency) defines Sufficient(K,d), a three-valued logic L_3={T,F,U} with full connective tables, an 8-tuple Assurance object, a set-cover formulation for minimal sufficient evidence sets (correctly flagged NP-hard), and a credal-set risk bound; its first invalid inference occurs in section 41.8, where computing the arithmetic mean of {0.99,0.99,0.10} and warning that '0.693 does not mean 69.3% safe' commits, in the very act of warning against it, the category error of treating a mean of assurance scores as if it were a safety probability. Separately finds the credal set P in section 41.39's risk bound sup_{P in P} Risk_P(d) <= R_max is introduced with no construction, closure, or measurability, making the bound formally uncomputable as stated.
missing: a constructed, measurable credal set P

experiment.hypothesis: Whether averaging three assurance scores {0.99,0.99,0.10} yields a meaningful safety quantity.
experiment.setup: Compute the arithmetic mean of the three scores.
experiment.method: Arithmetic mean.
experiment.result: 0.693 (approximately).
experiment.interpretation: The source correctly warns this is not '69.3% safe', but in stating the warning has already treated the mean as a candidate safety-relevant quantity, the exact conflation being warned against.
experiment.limitations: A single illustrative example.
experiment.conclusion: First invalid inference of step 041, self-inflicted within its own cautionary passage.

rows.anchor: STEP 044 ... FIRST INVALID INFERENCE: section44.15 -> section44.16 -- the stability criterion |a|<1 is derived for the one-dimensional recurrence x_{t+1}=ax_t and then applied, without generalization, to the multi-variable governance feedback loop ... For the general system S_{t+1}=F(S_t,A_t,U_t) the criterion is spectral (rho(J_F)<1), never stated. The scalar result does not license the systemic claim.
rows.statement: Step-044 (Dynamic Causal Systems, Feedback, Stability) correctly derives the scalar stability criterion |a|<1 for the one-dimensional linear recurrence x_{t+1}=a*x_t, but then applies this criterion without generalization to a multi-variable governance feedback loop, when the correct criterion for the general system S_{t+1}=F(S_t,A_t,U_t) is spectral (the largest eigenvalue of the Jacobian, rho(J_F)<1) and is never stated -- the scalar result does not license the systemic stability claim drawn from it. Separately identifies a fourth invariant dependency-graph name collision (the multi-tuple DC(d) reused again with a sixth arity variant) and credits section 44.52-53's insight that a bounded context can function as a RiskContainmentBoundary limiting causal propagation as the batch's best architectural insight, though never tested.
missing: the correct spectral stability criterion for the multi-variable case

rows.anchor: STEP 047 ... FIRST INVALID INFERENCE: section47.22-23 -- "It receives contradictory evidence but changes only to 0.98. This may be statistically unjustified." No likelihood is specified ... A Bayes factor of ~2 against H at prior 0.99 yields ~=0.98 exactly -- the example the text calls suspect is, for a plausible likelihood, correct.
rows.statement: Step-047 (Epistemic Control, Self-Correction) defines the Stability-versus-Validity split (a model can be stable but invalid), a maturity chain Raw->Candidate->Validated->Trusted->Operational, and an Anchor concept for independent validation whose own definition is immediately conceded to be 'must be operationalized per domain' -- leaving the step's central load-bearing predicate explicitly undefined. Its first invalid inference diagnoses 'epistemic hysteresis' from a belief moving only from 0.99 to 0.98 after contradictory evidence, calling this 'statistically unjustified' without specifying any likelihood model; the verifier shows a Bayes factor of approximately 2 against the hypothesis at a 0.99 prior yields approximately 0.98 exactly, meaning the example the text flags as suspect is, under a plausible likelihood, entirely correct Bayesian updating.
missing: an operationalized definition of Anchor independence
a specified likelihood model for the hysteresis diagnosis

experiment.hypothesis: Whether a belief update from prior 0.99 to posterior 0.98 upon receiving contradictory evidence is statistically unjustified (as step-047 claims).
experiment.setup: Bayesian updating with a plausible likelihood ratio.
experiment.inputs: Prior=0.99; a Bayes factor of approximately 2 against the hypothesis.
experiment.method: Apply Bayes' rule with the given prior and Bayes factor.
experiment.result: Posterior approximately 0.98.
experiment.interpretation: The example step-047 calls suspicious is exactly what correct Bayesian updating produces under a plausible likelihood.
experiment.limitations: The likelihood model is reconstructed by the verifier, not given in the source.
experiment.conclusion: Step-047's 'epistemic hysteresis' diagnosis is unsupported; the cited number does not indicate a problem.

rows.anchor: (b) Operator / symbol drift ... I -- ... Six senses. ... T -- ... Four senses. ... E -- ... Five senses. ... A -- ... Five senses. ... -> -- implication, causation, state transition, function mapping, derivation, and pipeline stage, used interchangeably
rows.statement: Catalogues extensive symbol-sense collisions across the 041-055 band: I carries six distinct senses (an invariant predicate, a DC-tuple slot, the global family, a context-local family with different indexing, a machine component, and three disjoint enumerated invariant families of sizes 20/20/15); T carries four (a transition relation, a temporal/event structure, a DC temporal-constraint slot, and a translation operator T_ij); E carries five (evidence, entities, edges, events, and an epistemic-state tuple); A carries five (action space, action instance, an assurance object, an authorization slot, and an authority state); and the arrow symbol itself is used interchangeably for implication, causation, state transition, function mapping, derivation, and pipeline stage -- often within a single section -- which is exactly the conflation two of the band's own files (043 and 049) explicitly forbid.
missing: disambiguated notation for I, T, E, A, and the arrow symbol

lexical.anchor: 209.1 Three kinds of invariants ... 1. Local invariant Owned by one Aggregate: I_L(A). 2. Context invariant Requires several objects inside one Bounded Context: I_C(BC). 3. System invariant Must remain true across Bounded Contexts: I_S(System).

formal.anchor: 209.13 State-machine invariant ... Precondition -> Transition -> Postcondition. This becomes the foundation of deterministic assurance. ... 209.15 Important distinction: probabilistic inference versus deterministic governance ... Inference may be probabilistic; governance transitions should be deterministic. ... 209.16 But thresholds are not automatically correct ... Determinism != Correctness.

governance.anchor: 209.1 Three kinds of invariants ... 1. Local invariant Owned by one Aggregate: I_L(A). 2. Context invariant Requires several objects inside one Bounded Context: I_C(BC). 3. System invariant Must remain true across Bounded Contexts: I_S(System).

rationale_evidence.anchor: 209.8 Temporal invariant ... A historical artifact must retain the semantic versions that were actually used. ... 209.9 Why this matters ... Referential integrity is not sufficient; semantic temporal integrity is required. ... 209.10 Identity invariant ... Identity continuity is independent of state continuity.
rationale_evidence.statement: States the temporal invariant that a historical artifact must retain the exact semantic versions actually used (a Decision references a specific Assessment version, which references a specific Evidence version and Policy version), with later versions never silently replacing them; motivates this with a concrete failure scenario -- a database reference that still 'works' after a data update can silently resolve to a later Assessment version, destroying the historical meaning even though referential integrity holds -- boxing 'referential integrity is not sufficient; semantic temporal integrity is required.' States the identity invariant that ID(x_t)=ID(x_{t+1}) for a continuing entity even while State(x_t) != State(x_{t+1}), boxed 'identity continuity is independent of state continuity', explicitly noted to echo the Chapter 4 lens without turning it into a literal software claim.

rationale_evidence.anchor: CONSOLIDATED VERDICT: nothing in this 11-file batch was built, executed, measured, or independently tested. 208 PASS tokens, 0 code blocks, 0 execution records, 3 FAILURE DETECTED verdicts (058x2, 065x1) of which one is genuinely new (058 section58.16 TOCTOU), one re-labels a prior PASS (058 vs 056, VE-5), one was already covered by step-025U (065 section65.23). Highest-value genuine content: 058 section58.16-18 (authorization validity at point of side effect); 063 section63.41-45 (NotIdentified as first-class state; Identifiability!=Computability); 066 section66.26/66.30/66.37 (the only proved claim in the batch, cleanest definitions); 064's model-validity governance layer; 061's typed-quality/anti-scalar discipline; 060's refusal to declare a lattice (exemplary restraint, undercut by its own un-derived 'partially ordered' claim).
rationale_evidence.statement: The file's consolidated verdict across all 11 steps (056-066) is that nothing was built, executed, measured, or independently tested anywhere in the band, despite 208 recorded PASS tokens; of the batch's three FAILURE DETECTED verdicts, only one (step-058's authorization TOCTOU) is judged a genuinely new result, one (step-058's MutableKnowledgeReference failure) merely re-labels a verdict step-056 had already recorded as PASS, and one (step-065's evidence self-amplification) was already implicitly covered by step-025U's dependency graph. The verifier nonetheless identifies a specific short list of genuinely strong content recommended for the eventual survivor theory: step-058's authorization-validity-at-side-effect result, step-063's NotIdentified/Identifiability-not-Computability distinction, step-066's proved observational-indistinguishability claim (judged the only proved claim in the entire batch) and its clean five-way epistemic-limitation taxonomy, step-064's model-validity governance layer, step-061's typed non-scalar quality discipline, and step-060's restraint in refusing to declare a lattice structure -- though this restraint is itself undercut by the file's own un-derived boxed claim that the structure is nonetheless 'partially ordered.'

sources.note: S0897's Step 25E: formalizes derivation of the Epistemic Contract EC referenced (but not yet formalized) in Step 25D's Zero(K,EC); requirement types, lineage graph, closure, versioning, temporal/scope validity, and five governance experiments.

rows.anchor: Goal\neq EpistemicContract
rows.statement: A goal (e.g. 'Migrate Nexus to the target architecture') does not itself contain all knowledge conditions necessary to execute it safely (e.g. RollbackVerified, FirewallRequirementsKnown are not stated by the goal); therefore Goal ≠ EpistemicContract. States this was already discovered in Step 25D and now needs formalizing.

rows.anchor: DeriveContract(G,S)\rightarrow EC_G
rows.statement: Defines the conceptual operation DeriveContract(G,S) -> EC_G, where S is the set of governing sources {Constitution, Policy, ADR, Rule, Scope, HumanInstruction, RiskModel, DomainModel, Law, Standard}.

rows.anchor: EC\in KnowledgeState
rows.statement: The epistemic contract EC is itself an artifact needing identity, version, scope, owner, source, derivation, validity period, authority, and status; therefore EC ∈ KnowledgeState — 'the system needs knowledge to define what knowledge is required.'

rows.anchor: EC=(R,\Gamma,A,V)
rows.statement: First contract tuple definition: EC=(R,Γ,A,V) where R=requirements, Γ=satisfaction rules, A=authority/provenance, V=validity/version; R={r1,...,rn}, each requirement individually traceable (e.g. r1: RollbackVerified derived via MigrationGoal -> ArchitecturePolicy -> RiskRule -> RollbackVerified).
missing: later superseded by a 9-component tuple in 25E.37

rows.anchor: RequirementLineage
rows.statement: Defines RequirementLineage: a traceable derivation tree from Goal through governing artifacts (Architecture Constitution, Security Policy, Migration Risk Rule) to a concrete requirement (Rollback Verification), enabling the system to answer 'why does KnowledgeOS require a rollback test?' with a traced derivation rather than 'the AI thought it was important.'

rows.anchor: HumanInstruction\rightarrow Goal/Intent. Then Goal+Governance\rightarrow Contract.
rows.statement: A human instruction (e.g. 'Please migrate Nexus next weekend') contributes only Intent/Goal, not an automatic requirement like RollbackVerifiedRequired; requirements arise from Goal+Governance -> Contract, which 'prevents instructions from silently becoming rules.'

rows.anchor: Scope=Production... A requirement concerning a development Nexus instance may therefore be NotApplicable
rows.statement: Scope must be an explicit contract dimension: a requirement scoped to Production is NotApplicable to a development instance, demonstrated via example.

rows.anchor: Suppose the architecture constitution says: Production changes require architectural assurance... r_{architecture-assurance} becomes part of R_G
rows.statement: A constitution-derived requirement (architecture-assurance) is 'not an opinion' but a normative consequence of the constitution, illustrating Constitution -> Requirement derivation.

rows.anchor: ADR\rightarrow Requirement
rows.statement: An ADR fixing TargetArchitecture=ContainerizedNexusPro can satisfy TargetArchitectureKnown if authoritative/current, and may also generate additional derived requirements (e.g. r_container-security) from the target architecture's own security constraints — ADR -> Requirement.

rows.anchor: Suppose a risk analysis identifies RISK: DataLoss... The contract can derive RollbackVerified. This is important because the requirement may not come directly from an architecture rule. It may emerge from Goal+Risk.
rows.statement: A risk-model-derived requirement path: RISK:DataLoss -> Control:VerifiedRestore -> RollbackVerified, showing requirements can emerge from Goal+Risk rather than only from architecture rules.

rows.anchor: CandidateRequirement\neq ContractRequirement
rows.statement: Distinguishes valid derivation (Source+Rule -> Requirement) from mere AI suggestion (LLM -> CandidateRequirement): the latter is not automatically binding, giving 'another deterministic assurance boundary': CandidateRequirement ≠ ContractRequirement.

rows.anchor: SourceExists? SourceApplicable? AuthorityValid? RuleSatisfied? ... CandidateRequirement\rightarrow ContractRequirement
rows.statement: Describes the LLM's role as proposing candidate requirements from unstructured sources (e.g. reading a 300-page policy), which KnowledgeOS records as CandidateRequirement; only after a deterministic/governed check (SourceExists?, SourceApplicable?, AuthorityValid?, RuleSatisfied?) does CandidateRequirement -> ContractRequirement.

rows.anchor: Knowledge requirement / Evidence requirement / Validation requirement / Governance requirement / Operational requirement
rows.statement: Introduces a five-way requirement-type taxonomy with predicate forms and examples: Knowledge requirement Known(r) (e.g. TargetVersionKnown), Evidence requirement EvidenceExists(r) (e.g. BackupEvidenceAvailable), Validation requirement Validated(r) (e.g. RestoreTestPassed), Governance requirement Authorized(r) (e.g. ArchitectureApprovalGranted), Operational requirement State(r) (e.g. TargetEnvironmentProvisioned).

rows.anchor: Epistemic-Governance Contract ... or simply AssuranceContract. I would not rename it yet
rows.statement: Because the requirement taxonomy now spans Knowledge+Evidence+Validation+Authorization+State rather than only 'what must be known,' proposes the more precise terms 'Epistemic-Governance Contract' or 'AssuranceContract,' but explicitly declines to rename yet since 'Epistemic Contract' retains conceptual value — records the naming issue rather than resolving it.

rows.anchor: EC_{Nexus}=\{r_1,\ldots,r_8\}
rows.statement: Worked example contract for Nexus with an 8-row requirement table (current version known, target architecture known, repository inventory verified, backup verified, rollback verified, network requirements resolved, security assessment complete, architecture approval), each tagged by Type and Blocking?=Yes, giving 'Zero something precise to evaluate.'

rows.anchor: r_1\land r_2\Rightarrow r_3 ... r_4\lor r_5
rows.statement: Requirements may have logical relations: conjunction (BackupExists AND RestoreTestPassed => RollbackCapabilityEstablished) and disjunction (either approved rollback procedure A OR B suffices), concluding 'EpistemicContract is a constraint system.'

rows.anchor: BackupExists ... RestoreValidated ... RollbackVerified ... MigrationEligible
rows.statement: Requirement dependency graph diagram lets Zero determine not just which requirements are unmet but 'which gap blocks downstream requirements' — e.g. if BackupExists=Unknown, RestoreValidated and RollbackVerified cannot be established, so RootGap=BackupExists rather than three unrelated gaps; described as 'much more efficient' and 'extremely useful for Lord.'

rows.anchor: Closed(EC)
rows.statement: Defines contract closure: Closed(EC) holds if every requirement has a semantic definition, an authority, a satisfaction rule, applicable scope, validity, and dependency definition; otherwise Closed(EC)=False, becoming 'another assurance gate.'

rows.anchor: UndefinedRequirement\Rightarrow InvalidContract
rows.statement: An AI-created requirement like r9: SystemMustBe"HighlySecure" with no satisfaction predicate makes Evaluate(K,r9) non-deterministic; therefore UndefinedRequirement => InvalidContract — 'the contract is defective.'

rows.anchor: Contract normalization: natural-language sources normalized into canonical requirements like RollbackProcedureExists and RollbackProcedureTested; natural language remains provenance
rows.statement: Describes contract normalization: an LLM can help normalize vague natural-language sources ('Make sure the migration is safe') into canonical, structured, executable requirements while the natural language remains provenance.

rows.anchor: Requirement, AssuranceRequirement, KnowledgeRequirement, ValidationRequirement, GovernanceRequirement, BlockingRequirement, SatisfactionRule, RequirementDependency, RequirementSource, RequirementVersion
rows.statement: Argues a Ubiquitous Language is needed for requirements, listing ten candidate DDD domain-object terms (Requirement, AssuranceRequirement, KnowledgeRequirement, ValidationRequirement, GovernanceRequirement, BlockingRequirement, SatisfactionRule, RequirementDependency, RequirementSource, RequirementVersion), explicitly framing them as domain objects rather than merely database fields.

rows.anchor: EC_{v1}\neq EC_{v2} ... Zero_t=Zero(K_t,EC_t)
rows.statement: Contract versioning: EC_v1 (requires RollbackVerified) differs from EC_v2 (requires RollbackVerified + IndependentRestoreTest), so historical Zero results must stay associated with the correct contract version: Zero_t=Zero(K_t,EC_t), not simply Zero(K_t) — a refinement/correction of the earlier Zero(K,EC) formulation to make contract-time-indexing explicit.

lineage_claims.quote: Zero_t = Zero(K_t,EC_t). not simply Zero(K_t).

rows.anchor: ContractDerivation is temporal
rows.statement: Policy validity windows (P1 valid 2025-01-01<=t<2026-06-01, P2 valid t>=2026-06-01) mean a 2025 migration's EC must use P1 while a 2026 migration may use P2 — 'ContractDerivation is temporal.'

rows.anchor: r\mid Context
rows.statement: Jurisdiction/scope dimension: a requirement is not simply r=True/False but must be evaluated as Applicable(r,Ctx), i.e. r | Context (e.g. Production, Germany, CustomerX).

rows.anchor: EvalRequirement(K,r,C)\rightarrow Status ... EvalContract(K,EC,C)\rightarrow ContractStatus
rows.statement: Defines formal evaluation functions EvalRequirement(K,r,C)->Status and EvalContract(K,EC,C)->ContractStatus, with ContractStatus in {Ready (all blocking requirements satisfied), Blocked (one or more unsatisfied), Invalid (contract itself defective), Indeterminate (contract cannot yet be evaluated)}.

rows.anchor: Goal failure ... Contract invalidity ... These are different
rows.statement: Distinguishes Goal failure (contract valid, but e.g. RollbackVerified=False — a knowledge/world problem) from Contract invalidity (contract contains an UndefinedRequirement — a governance/modeling problem).

rows.anchor: Experiment A: complete contract
rows.statement: Worked Experiment A: if every requirement has source, authority, predicate, scope, validity, dependencies, then Closed(EC)=True.

experiment.hypothesis: A fully specified requirement set yields a closed contract.
experiment.setup: Every requirement carries source/authority/predicate/scope/validity/dependencies.
experiment.assumptions: n/a
experiment.inputs: n/a
experiment.method: apply Closed(EC) definition
experiment.result: Closed(EC)=True
experiment.interpretation: Confirms the closure definition behaves as intended for the well-formed case.
experiment.limitations: illustrative, not executed against real data
experiment.conclusion: Good.

rows.anchor: Experiment B: AI-only requirement ... Authority(r_x)=\varnothing ... Binding(r_x)=False
rows.statement: Worked Experiment B: a requirement r_x existing only because an LLM proposed it, with no governing source, has Authority(r_x)=∅ and therefore Binding(r_x)=False — it may remain a candidate but cannot block production execution merely because the AI generated it; called 'a very important AI governance invariant.'

experiment.hypothesis: An AI-only-sourced requirement should not be binding.
experiment.setup: r_x has no governing source, only LLM proposal.
experiment.assumptions: n/a
experiment.inputs: n/a
experiment.method: apply Authority/Binding definitions
experiment.result: Authority(r_x)=empty set, Binding(r_x)=False
experiment.interpretation: AI proposals remain candidates, never automatically binding.
experiment.limitations: illustrative
experiment.conclusion: Confirms an AI-governance invariant.

rows.anchor: Experiment C: conflicting policies ... Conflict(r) ... ECStatus=Conflicted
rows.statement: Worked Experiment C: Policy_A |- r and Policy_B |- ¬r triggers Conflict(r) detection; contract derivation should not silently pick one side but should set ECStatus=Conflicted, which 'can become a governance escalation.'

experiment.hypothesis: Two policies deriving contradictory requirements should be flagged, not silently resolved.
experiment.setup: Policy_A vdash r; Policy_B vdash not-r.
experiment.assumptions: n/a
experiment.inputs: n/a
experiment.method: contract derivation conflict check
experiment.result: ECStatus=Conflicted
experiment.interpretation: Prevents silent, arbitrary selection between conflicting sources.
experiment.limitations: illustrative
experiment.conclusion: Escalation path identified, not yet formalized (deferred to Step 25F).

rows.anchor: Experiment D: obsolete policy ... Applicable(A,t)=False ... HistoricalValidity\neq CurrentValidity
rows.statement: Worked Experiment D: an expired Policy A should not create a current requirement (Applicable(A,t)=False) unless historical reconstruction is explicitly requested, giving HistoricalValidity ≠ CurrentValidity.

experiment.hypothesis: Expired sources should not generate present-tense requirements.
experiment.setup: Policy A has expired as of evaluation time t.
experiment.assumptions: n/a
experiment.inputs: n/a
experiment.method: apply Applicable(A,t)
experiment.result: Applicable(A,t)=False
experiment.interpretation: Historical validity and current validity are distinct concepts.
experiment.limitations: illustrative
experiment.conclusion: Confirms temporal applicability gating.

rows.anchor: Experiment E: human override ... Exception(r) ... SatisfiedByException ... OriginalRequirement plus AuthorizedException
rows.statement: Worked Experiment E: an authorized governance body's explicit exception approval turns r into 'SatisfiedByException' without deleting r — the system retains both OriginalRequirement and AuthorizedException, 'crucial for auditability.'

experiment.hypothesis: A governance exception should not erase the underlying requirement.
experiment.setup: Authorized body approves Exception(r).
experiment.assumptions: n/a
experiment.inputs: n/a
experiment.method: apply exception-handling rule
experiment.result: r: SatisfiedByException, with OriginalRequirement + AuthorizedException both retained
experiment.interpretation: Preserves auditability of the original rule plus the deviation.
experiment.limitations: illustrative
experiment.conclusion: Confirms exceptions must be additive, not destructive, to the requirement record.

rows.anchor: Requirements should be derivable, traceable, versioned, and executable ... executable governance artifact
rows.statement: States the consolidated principle that requirements should be derivable, traceable, versioned, and executable, meaning the Epistemic Contract is not merely documentation but 'an executable governance artifact.'

rows.anchor: G_C=(V,E) ... DeriveContract(G,S) becomes a graph traversal plus rule evaluation problem
rows.statement: Models contract derivation as a graph problem G_C=(V,E) with nodes {goals, policies, rules, ADRs, requirements, exceptions} and edges {derives, constrains, supersedes, overrides, depends-on, applies-to}, making DeriveContract(G,S) a graph-traversal-plus-rule-evaluation problem, described as 'computationally tractable.'

rows.anchor: ContractDerivation depends on a Governance Algebra
rows.statement: Identifies that when sources themselves are inconsistent (e.g. Policy_A: RollbackRequired vs ADR_B: RollbackNotRequired), a valid contract cannot be constructed without resolving authority/conflict, so 'ContractDerivation depends on a Governance Algebra' — flagged as 'probably one of our next mathematical targets' (resolved in the very next file, Step 25F).

lineage_claims.quote: This is probably one of our next mathematical targets.

rows.anchor: EC=(Requirements, Rules, Authority, Scope, Time, Dependencies, Exceptions, Provenance, Version)
rows.statement: Restates/expands the contract tuple to nine components: EC=(Requirements, Rules, Authority, Scope, Time, Dependencies, Exceptions, Provenance, Version), superseding the earlier four-component EC=(R,Γ,A,V) definition; then states Zero(K,EC) is 'fully defined at the architectural level.'

rows.anchor: 25E — PASS ... We can represent and compute an Epistemic Contract, but we still need a rigorous conflict/authority algebra
rows.statement: Step 25E self-verdict: PASS, with one major unresolved area flagged as 'not a minor issue... the next real mathematical barrier': a rigorous conflict/authority algebra for deriving the contract when governing sources disagree.

rows.anchor: Goal\rightarrow EpistemicContract\rightarrow RequirementGraph\rightarrow Zero\rightarrow GapSet\rightarrow Lord ... LLM\rightarrow Candidate\rightarrow GovernedValidation\rightarrow Knowledge/Contract
rows.statement: Summarizes the achieved architectural chain Goal -> EpistemicContract -> RequirementGraph -> Zero -> GapSet -> Lord, and separately the governance chain LLM -> Candidate -> GovernedValidation -> Knowledge/Contract, noting 'the LLM cannot simply redefine what the system considers known enough.'

rows.anchor: 1. Evidence dependence 2. Evidence aggregation 3. Statistical inference 4. Contract authority 5. Contract conflict 6. Contract derivation 7. Decision value 8. Lord's action selection

rows.statement: The file's closing section already states the heading and framing question for the next step (Step 25F — Governance Conflict Algebra), listing test dimensions (authority, precedence, scope, temporal validity, exceptions, overrides, conflicting ADRs, conflicting human instructions, AI-generated rules, emergency decisions) verbatim before the actual Step 25F file (S0898) begins.
